newsitem.title: USA: ANALYSIS--US retail sales point to 4 pct Q1 growth.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS--US retail sales point to 4 pct Q1 growth.

text.p: Thursday's U.S. retail sales report could leave economists scrambling to revise upward their estimates for first quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth, experts said.

February retail sales came in close to expectations, up 0.8 percent and up 0.5 percent excluding automobile sales. But January's revisions were the most dramatic this highly volatile figure had shown in more than a year, to up 1.5 percent from up 0.6 and excluding autos to up 1.4 percent from up 0.4 percent.

The January revision along with strong February figures could portend 4.0 percent GDP growth in the first quarter of 1997, according to William Sullivan, director of money market research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
"Everybody that's credible has to revise first quarter GDP estimates upward. This report shows that imbalances may be developing," Sullivan said.

He said households clearly were spending more than income growth dictated, perhaps the result of cashing in on stock market profits or just symbolic of the increased security Americans are feeling about their jobs and economic prospects.
"If the Fed were looking for imbalances they may have finally found one. These are very formidable figures," Sullivan said.

"I wouldn't be surprised if the bond traded at 7.0 percent by the end of today. Consumer spending is a lot stronger than expected," added Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.

Platt said he was in the process of revising upward his first quarter GDP forecast based on the strength of retail sales. "They're not necessarily a sign of imbalances, but they are one more reason for the Fed to tighten," he said.
"This was another indication of strength in the economy, particularly on the ex-autos side," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities Inc.

Levenson said sales strength was indicative of 4.0 percent or higher first quarter GDP growth and provided the Fed with more ammunition to tighten, making such a move at its policymaking meeting on March 25 more likely than not.

"If (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan thinks risk valuations in the credit markets have been too low and this is now feeding through with stronger consumer demand," it probably was enough to convince him of the necessity of tightening, Levenson said.
